extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and graduate students preparing research papers and journal submissions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and editorial rules for writing, shortening, and polishing mathematical research papers, including model phrases for editorial correspondence and referees plus detailed English-grammar usage relevant to mathematical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for an expert; delete trivial or routine material
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember: you are writing for an expert. Cross out all that is trivial or routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule to shorten papers by removing material an expert reader already knows; focus on new contributions. (Original: "Remember: you are writing for an expert. Cross out all that is trivial or routine.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetition of assumptions, conclusions and formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repetition: do not repeat the assumptions of a theorem at the beginning of its proof, or a complicated conclusion at the end of the proof. Do not repeat the assumptions of a previous theorem in the statement of a next one (instead, write e.g. “Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1 with f replaced by g, .....”). Do not repeat the same formula—use a label instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When referencing earlier material, refer to it concisely (e.g. "Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1 with f replaced by g"). Label formulas and reuse labels rather than copying expressions. This reduces length and increases clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check necessity of every formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Check all formulas: is each of them necessary?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When shortening, critically evaluate whether each displayed or inline formula contributes to the argument or could be omitted or summarized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrases you can cross out
rubrics_metrics.description: List of verbose introductory or redundant phrases that can be removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided to delete entirely: "We denote by R the set of all real numbers.", "We have the following lemma.", "The following lemma will be useful.", "..... the following inequality is satisﬁed:". Use terse mathematical language and avoid filler sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrases you can shorten
rubrics_metrics.description: Common verbose formulations and their concise alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many explicit substitutions given (see p. 38 referenced). Examples: "Let ε be an arbitrary but ﬁxed positive number" → "Fix ε > 0"; "Let us ﬁrst observe that" → "First observe that"; "By virtue of (4)" → "By (4)"; "In the interval [0, 1]" → "In [0, 1]"; "A function of class C 2" → "A C^2 function"; "Applying Lemma 1 we conclude that" → "Lemma 1 shows that"; and other pairings. Use the shorter forms routinely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard concise editorial correspondence phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred concise phrases for submitting, withdrawing, thanking, and corresponding about manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model lines to use in letters: "I would like to submit" / "I am submitting"; "the enclosed manuscript '.....' for publication in Studia Mathematica."; "Please ﬁnd enclosed two copies of the revised version."; "As the referee suggested, I inserted a reference to the theorem of ....."; "I have complied with almost all suggestions of the referee." Also polite withdrawal/acceptance lines: "I wish to withdraw my paper ..... as I intend to make a major revision of it."; "Thank you very much for accepting my paper for publication in ....." Use these concise forms rather than long paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee's report: positive, critical and rejection phrasings
rubrics_metrics.description: Model sentences and typical evaluative comments for writing referee reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of positive phrasing: "The author proves the interesting result that .....", "The proof is short and simple, and the article well written.", "The results presented are original.", "I strongly recommend it for publication in Studia Mathematica." Critical phrasing examples: "The only remark I wish to make is that condition B should be formulated more carefully.", "A few minor typographical errors are listed below.", "The English of the paper needs a thorough revision." Rejection phrasing: "Accordingly, I recommend that the paper be rejected.", "Theorem 2 is false as stated.", "The results obtained are not particularly surprising and will be of limited interest." Use specific, concise judgments and give evidence/examples for criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the indefinite article (a, an, —)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for when to use 'a' or 'an' and common uses of indefinite article in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: choose a/an by pronunciation (e.g., 'a unit', 'an x'). Guidelines include: (1) Use instead of the number 'one' (e.g., 'A chapter will be devoted ...'); (2) To mean 'member of a class', 'some', 'one of' (examples throughout); (3) In definitions of classes of objects ("A fundamental solution is ..."); plural variants illustrated; many concrete examples provided for mathematical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the definite article (the)
rubrics_metrics.description: When to use 'the' (meaning 'mentioned earlier', uniquely determined object, in construction, in front of surnames used attributively, in plural to refer to a class as a whole, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules numbered 1–7 include examples: "Let A ⊂ X. If aB = 0 for every B intersecting the set A, then ..."; "the Dirichlet problem", "the Taylor expansion"; use 'the' when referring to a uniquely determined object or to refer to a whole class in the plural ("The real measures form a subclass ..."). Contrast cases where 'the' should be omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article omission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when to omit articles (a/an/the) in mathematical English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed examples and cases (1–10): omit before nouns referring to activities ("Application of Definition 5.9 gives (45)."), before nouns referring to properties when no particular object is mentioned, after certain 'of' expressions ("a type of convergence"), in front of numbered objects ("It follows from Theorem 7 that ..."), to avoid repetition, before surnames in the possessive, in some descriptive expressions after 'with' and 'of', after forms of 'have' ("It has finite norm."), in front of the name of a mathematical discipline ("in the theory of distributions"), and other examples. Use these patterns to decide article omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitive uses and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when and how to use infinitives ('to' + verb) in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules and examples numbered 1–10: (1) Indicating aim or intention ("To prove the theorem, we first let ..."), (2) constructions with 'too' and 'enough' ("too complicated to be used"), (3) indicating one action leads to another, (4) constructions like 'we may assume M to be ...', (5) 'M is assumed to be ...' with possible verbs, (6) in structures like 'for this to happen', (7) as subject of a sentence ("To see that ... is fairly easy."), (8) after forms of 'be' ("Our goal is to find ..."), (9) replacing relative clauses ("The theorem to be proved is ..."), (10) after certain verbs ("He proposed to study that problem."). Additional notes on specific verbs ('enable' requires explicit subject).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of the -ing form (gerund/participle)
rubrics_metrics.description: When to use ing-forms as subjects, after prepositions, in separate clauses, describing nouns, and other constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules 1–8 with examples: (1) as subject without 'the' ("Repeating the previous argument ..."), (2) after prepositions ("After making a linear transformation ..."), (3) in expressions with 'of' ("The idea of combining (2) and (3) ..."), (4) after certain verbs especially with prepositions ("We begin by analyzing (3)."), (5) present participle in a separate clause (subject consistency rule), (6) present participle describing a noun ("a function with image having support in ..."), (7) when rephraseable by 'where' or 'since' ("Now J is defined to equal Af, the function f being as in (3)."), (8) expressions rephrased as 'the fact that X is ...' ("Note that M being cyclic implies F is cyclic."). Use examples to choose between ing-form and alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of passive voice in mathematical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on appropriate passive constructions and how passive replaces certain 'we' structures or marks future/expected proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items 1–6: (1) usual passive ("This theorem was proved by Milnor in 1976."), (2) passive to replace 'we do something' ("This identity is established by ..."), (3) to replace 'we prove that X is' ("The function M is easily shown to have ..."), (4) to express 'we give an object X a structure Y' ("E can be given a complex structure by ..."), (5) to express 'we act on something' ("This order behaves well when g is acted upon by an operator."), (6) meaning 'which will be (proved etc.)' ("Before stating the result to be proved, we give ..."). Use passive for objectivity, but be mindful of clarity and subject-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier usage and common pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and examples for quantifier words (all, every, each, there exists, none, no, both, either, neither, etc.) and correct agreement with singular/plural nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive examples demonstrating proper usage: "all open subsets of U", "for every g in X there exists an N ..."; notes on 'every' followed by singular noun, inversion after negative clauses, difference between 'each' and 'every', use of 'any' vs 'any given', and constructions like 'all extend to a neighbourhood of U'. Also cautions: do not write 'Every subspace is not ...' when you mean 'No subspace is ...'. Ensure quantifier choice matches intended logical scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number, quantity and size expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on cardinal and ordinal numbers, fractions, comparative expressions, multiples, superlatives, and numeric phrasing in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 1–11 cover many points: cardinal numbers ("There are at most 2 such r"), ordinal usage ("the first two"), fraction expressions ("Two-thirds of its diameter"; note 'half' can be used with or without 'of'), comparisons ('greater than', 'no greater than', 'strictly less than'), 'how many times as great' ("twice as long as"), multiples ("k-fold integration"), superlatives ("the least such constant is called the norm"), 'many/few/a number of' usage, equality/difference phrasing, numbering conventions ("Exercises 2 to 5"), and examples. Use the precise mathematical phrasing illustrated to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to avoid repetition (nouns, adjectives, verbs, sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategies and phrasing to avoid needless repetition in mathematical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and many examples: replace repeated nouns by pronouns or phrases like 'the former/the latter' ("Both f and g are connected, but the latter is in addition compact."); avoid repeating adjectives and adverbs; compress repeated verbs and sentence structures; avoid repeating whole sentences by using 'the same holds for ...' or 'the same being true for ...'. Replace lists of similar objects by 'whichever is the larger of the two' rather than 'the two ones'. Use concise cross-references to earlier results instead of restating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word order and adverb placement
rubrics_metrics.description: General remarks on normal English word order in mathematical sentences and detailed guidance on placement of adverbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule: subject + verb + direct object + adverbs in manner-place-time order. Detailed subrules for adverb placement: (1a) frequency adverbs (between subject and verb or after auxiliaries), (1a) adverbs like 'also/therefore' (examples: "Our presentation is therefore organized ..."), (1a) emphatic adverbs ("It would clearly have been sufficient ..."), (1b) after verb (adverbs of manner: "One sees immediately ..."), (1c) after a short object ("We will prove the theorem directly ..."), (1d) sentence-initial adverbs referring to whole sentence ("Incidentally, ...", "Finally, ..."). Use these placements to produce idiomatic, clear mathematical prose.
